newsitem.title: USA: US Senate tax outline seeks 501(c)(3) cap increase.
newsitem.headline: US Senate tax outline seeks 501(c)(3) cap increase.

text.p: A broad outline of proposals for the Senate Finance Committee's tax bill calls for increasing the current $150 million limit on issuance of so-called 501(c)(3) bonds for new financings.
The six-page discussion paper, obtained by Reuters, was distributed to senators and does not discuss other tax issues of specific interest to the tax-exempt bond market.

Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, R-Del., plans to unveil his tax bill next week. The discussion paper was described as the direction the bill is taking but specifics are still being worked out.

The House Ways and Means Committee early Friday approved tax legislation that would raise the limit on non-hospital borrowing by 501(c)(3) groups from the current $150 million to $200 million over five years.
The Senate Finance outline simply states: "The $150 million limitation on 501(c)(3) bonds will be increased for new financings."
A 501(c)(3) bond generally is issued by a nonprofit group that qualifies for an exemption from federal tax, such as universities, housing authorities, and hospitals.

According to the tax outline, Congress' Joint Committee on Taxation tentatively estimated that the provisions would cost the U.S. Treasury about $30 billion over five years and $75 billion over 10 years, the outline says.
The outline appears to discuss only those provisions that would produce a cost for the U.S. government, called "revenue losers". It does not discuss so-called "revenue raisers".
The outline would increase exemptions from the alternative minimum tax (AMT) for individuals annually - by $450 for singles and $600 for married couples - after 2001.
It does not, however, mention repeal of the corporate alternative minimum tax (AMT).

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer on Thursday agreed to drop his proposal to repeal the corporate AMT, disappointing muni bond groups who said that repeal would trigger increased demand for long-term municipals by property and casualty companies.
The outline also does not mention proposals sought by bond lobbyists groups to simplify the so-called arbitrage rebate process for municipalities that issue tax-exempt bonds.

Arbitrage is made by selling tax-exempt bonds and reinvesting the proceeds in higher yielding securities. The Internal Revenue Service requires issuers to calculate whether they earned excess funds and reimburse the U.S. if necessary.
Municipal groups say the comples process is costly and want the U.S. to simplify it and to exempt more issuers from the task.
